Shown while your position is being shared with the family.
The family can see where you are.
Where the satellites are jammed, the phone is told it is somewhere it cannot be, and the marker jumps across the map. This leaves out any position that would have taken more than 200 km/h to reach.

Which kinds of answer count towards the point this phone reports. An answer from a source switched off is still collected and logged, but it moves no marker and reaches no one. Where the satellites are jammed, leaving only the towers and the Wi-Fi is the sensible setting: a wider answer, but not a false one. With every switch off the phone writes nothing at all.
Sharing needs access to this phone\'s position. Allow it in the application settings.
Allow notifications, so that a running service can say so.
To keep sharing while the application is closed, set the location access to \"Allow all the time\" in the application settings.
Nobody has shared a position yet.
Had not settled since the phone was switched on
Drift while the phone lay still
A speed the phone was never carried at
Too much doubt in the answer
The track goes round a circle
The signal is not from orbit
Not set: the model is shown
Everyone who sees this device sees this name.
Heard for nothing: %1$s. The receiver holds no orbit for any of those satellites, which is what erasing the aiding data puts right.

The phone holds every position against several rules and rejects it as soon as the first one speaks. A rejection is not a fault: where the signal is spoofed there are more rejected answers than accepted ones, and that is the work being done properly.
The phone named the radius it is somewhere inside, and the radius is over half a kilometre.
Such an answer names a district rather than a place. It is what the towers give while the phone is indoors.
Reaching this place from the last one in the time between them would have taken over 200 km/h.
One of the two is false. A spoof throws the marker far off rather than easing it along.
Two different positions arrived carrying the same moment.
The source is contradicting itself, which is what happens when a receiver is caught between a transmitter on the ground and the satellites.
The answer landed in an area you marked as somewhere the spoof puts phones.
A transmitter puts the marker there, not the satellites. The areas belong to the group, so marking one from any phone is enough.
The movement sensors say the phone was not carried anywhere, and the position changed.
Only a false signal moves the marker of a phone lying still: steps and journeys are counted by a chip of their own that a transmitter cannot reach.
The phone is lying where it was put down, and the answers walk away from it a little at a time.
A slow drift. A step of thirty metres never trips a comparison between neighbours, but within an hour the marker is somewhere else, so the distance is counted from where the phone was put down.
The phone has not been touched, and the answer says it is travelling at the speed of a car.

The receiver reports a speed of its own alongside every position, and on a phone lying still that speed is zero. A false signal draws a road and a speed along it, and the speed is inside the single answer — so this catches the first false position rather than the one after it.
The position from the satellites and the position from the towers and the Wi-Fi are kilometres apart.
The towers are harder to imitate than the satellites. This is the one rule that does not compare an answer with an earlier one, so it catches both a slow drift and the very first false answer.
The answers go round a closed circle at a steady speed.
Every stretch of such a track reads as ordinary driving. What gives it away is that the road closes, which is how a transmitter draws one and not how anybody drives.
The phone has been through this same run of places before.
A recorded false route is being played through again.
The fix rests on the satellites of the 1575 MHz band — GPS, Galileo, BeiDou — while GLONASS is heard and left out of it.
A spoofing transmitter works in one band. GLONASS broadcasts at 1602 MHz, out of its reach, so the receiver could not reconcile it with the satellites it was handed.
Every satellite arrives at the same strength however low it claims to be, and the far band is silent.
A real sky grows quieter the lower the satellite. One strength for all of them means one point on the ground.
Between two epochs the time the satellites carry advanced by a different amount than the phone\'s own clock did.
The phone counts the seconds since it was switched on, and nothing transmitted can reach that count. A signal built to move the phone has to move the time it carries, and the step shows up here.
The first five minutes after the phone was switched on, while the answer rests on fewer than four satellites.
In those minutes the receiver reports places the phone has never been. Answers of that window are held to tighter limits: wider than a hundred metres, or faster than 5 m/s, and they are rejected.
You switched this source of a position off in the settings.
Nothing is wrong with the answer: it is collected and logged, but it moves no marker and reaches nobody. That is what the switch is for.
The orbits and the last known place the receiver searches by. Aiding data gone wrong keeps a whole constellation out of every answer: its satellites are heard and none of them count.

The receiver starts again from nothing: the first position takes minutes instead of seconds, and the orbits are gathered back over the quarter of an hour that follows. Worth doing when a constellation is heard for days without ever entering the answer.
The phone keeps its own list of applications allowed to start. Nothing can read it, so mark it yourself once it is set.
You are not in a group yet. Make one and hand out an invitation, or paste in the invitation somebody sent you.
The invitation lets somebody in for a day, and lets in everybody it reaches in that time. Send it whole: it names the group as well as the code.
Nobody runs this group, so its members are set from the Firebase console.
The database refused that. The invitation may have run out, or the group may already exist.
Nobody else has signed in yet.
How a phone collects its position
The phone chooses one of these five by itself. Somebody with the map open outranks everything else; the rest of the time it spends as little as it can and still be found.
Asks for the most exact position every 15 seconds, and writes it as soon as the marker would move.
The phone noticed walking, running, cycling or riding.
Away from where it last wrote, with nobody looking.
Between 23:00 and 07:00, or the charge is below 15 per cent.
Asks every 20 minutes, in the cheapest way it has.
Settled within 150 metres of the position it last wrote.
Asks for nothing at all, and repeats the last position every 25 minutes so the card does not go grey.
